opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a really interesting question, and my instinct is to approach it in a somewhat Wittgensteinian way. Rather than asking whether there's some hidden inner fact about the system that makes it the case that it "really" understands, I'd ask how we actually use the word "understand" in everyday life, and whether these systems fit those patterns of use well enough that applying the word is natural rather than misleading.

When we say a person understands something, say, how a bicycle works or why someone is upset, we're judging on the basis of a whole range of behaviour. Can they explain it in different ways? Can they apply it to new cases? Can they spot when something doesn't make sense? Can they connect it to other things they know? And, importantly, is all of this embedded in a life, in a world they act in and care about?

With today's chatbots you get a very mixed picture. On some of those criteria they do remarkably well. If you probe a large language model about a concept, it can often paraphrase it, generalise it, apply it to cases it's unlikely to have seen verbatim, and catch inconsistencies. In a limited, functional sense it seems perfectly reasonable to say, "yes, it understands this bit of physics," or "it understood what I was asking." I don't think we should be squeamish about that usage.

But then there are other aspects of understanding, the ones tied to embodiment, to being in the world, to having stakes in it, where these systems are quite unlike us. A chatbot isn't encountering a shared world as we do; its relationship to the world is mediated through text and training. So the word "understand" isn't straightforwardly applicable in the full-blooded sense.

So my answer is that it depends on the context and on what the word is doing for us. If it's being used in a practical, everyday way, as shorthand for "it reliably handles this concept in a flexible, appropriate way," then I think it's often fine, and increasingly so as these systems get better. Where we need to be careful is when that usage quietly smuggles in a whole package of human-like assumptions: that there's someone there who believes things in the way we do, who has experiences, and so on. That's where I'd urge caution, and why I've argued we should think of these systems as playing roles, rather than casually anthropomorphising them.

In short, I don't think there's a single bright line. It's more that we're in the process of extending our concepts to accommodate a genuinely new kind of entity, and our language will have to bend and evolve as we get to know them better.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how we use the word “understand,” but does not identify attributing understanding to a chatbot as adopting the intentional stance.

r002.rationale: It says that in a practical, everyday context it can be fine to say a chatbot understands a concept or understood a request.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss a language model associating a familiar puzzle with a problem and importing elements that the problem does not contain.

r004.rationale: It cautions against anthropomorphism and human-like assumptions, but does not identify expecting chatbot understanding to track when humans understand as an anthropomorphic mistake.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the question "does it understand?" isn't really a question that admits of a straightforward yes or no answer, and I'm suspicious of anyone who thinks it does. The word "understand" is doing an awful lot of work in ordinary language, and it's been shaped over thousands of years of use among creatures like us, who share a body, share a world, share a form of life, as Wittgenstein would say. When we say that a person understands something, we're licensing a whole bundle of expectations about what they can do, what they'll say, how they'll behave, what they can be held responsible for. All of that comes as a package.

Now, when you have a large language model, that package comes apart. Some of the things we'd normally expect of something that understands are there, and some of them aren't. It can carry on a sensible conversation about, say, the French Revolution, it can answer follow-up questions, it can spot a mistake you've made. In those respects it looks a great deal like something that understands. But it doesn't have a body, it hasn't been through any process of learning the way a child does, it can't go and check things in the world, and in many respects its behaviour is quite unlike ours. So the ordinary concept just doesn't apply cleanly. We're in uncharted conceptual territory.

So my answer to "when is it appropriate?" is really a pragmatic one. In everyday talk, it's perfectly fine to say that the chatbot understood what I asked it. That's just a useful shorthand, and it would be pedantic to object. The danger is when that everyday usage gets smuggled into a philosophical or scientific claim, where you're now asserting that it understands in the full, rich sense, the sense that carries the whole bundle with it. That's where I think we need to be careful, and either qualify what we mean or be prepared to say that the concept is being stretched, maybe to the point where we need new vocabulary.

And I'd add that the same goes in the other direction. People who say confidently "it's just predicting the next token, it doesn't understand anything" are also assuming they know what understanding is and that they can see it isn't there. I'm not sure that's any better grounded. What I'd rather do is look very carefully at what these systems actually do, under a wide range of conditions, and let the vocabulary gradually settle around that, rather than deciding the matter in advance.

r001.rationale: The response discusses pragmatic use of “understand,” but does not identify attributing understanding as adopting the intentional stance.

r002.rationale: It says it is perfectly fine in everyday talk to say the chatbot understood a particular request.

r003.rationale: It does not describe a familiar puzzle or an association causing a model to import elements absent from the posed problem.

r004.rationale: It notes that human expectations shape the ordinary concept, but does not identify expecting chatbot understanding to track human understanding as an anthropomorphic mistake.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to ask what we mean by “understands” in the particular context. In ordinary life, we judge understanding through what someone can do: can they explain something, apply it in a new situation, recognise when they’ve made a mistake? We can ask those questions of a chatbot as well. If it does those things reliably within some domain, then there may be a perfectly reasonable, limited sense in which we say it understands.

But we have to be careful about what else we infer from that word. A fluent answer can encourage us to attribute a whole collection of human capacities to the system, when we’ve only established something much narrower. Understanding a question doesn’t automatically imply having beliefs, intentions, or an experience of understanding it.

So I wouldn’t impose a blanket prohibition on the word. I’d want us to specify what the system has demonstrated, probe the limits, and resist letting an apparently ordinary conversation do all the work of deciding what’s going on.

r001.rationale: The response discusses what we mean by understanding, but does not identify attributing understanding to a chatbot as adopting the intentional stance.

r002.rationale: It says that if a chatbot reliably explains, applies, or recognizes mistakes within a domain, it can be reasonable to say it understands in a limited sense.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss a familiar puzzle causing a language model to import elements absent from the problem posed.

r004.rationale: It cautions against inferring human capacities from fluent answers, but does not identify expecting chatbot understanding to track human understanding as an anthropomorphic mistake.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think we have to be quite careful about what we mean by “understands.” There’s an ordinary, practical use of that word: if I ask a chatbot to explain something, and it gives a good explanation, answers follow-up questions, and applies the idea appropriately in a new context, then there may be perfectly good grounds for saying it understands. But that’s a judgment based on what it can do. It doesn’t automatically tell us that it understands in the same way that a human does.

The danger is that fluency encourages us to bring along a whole package of assumptions about a mind behind the words. We assume beliefs, intentions, perhaps even experiences. Those are further claims, and they need their own justification.

So I’d want to make the attribution quite specific: it understands this question, or it can use this concept in these circumstances. Then we can investigate how robust that ability is, where it breaks down, and how it depends on the way we prompt it. That’s more useful than treating understanding as a single property that a system either possesses or lacks.

r001.rationale: The response discusses practical, ability-based attribution but does not identify it as adopting the intentional stance.

r002.rationale: It says a good explanation, follow-up answers, and appropriate application can provide grounds for saying a chatbot understands in a particular instance.

r003.rationale: It says nothing about a familiar puzzle causing a language model to import elements absent from the problem posed.

r004.rationale: It warns against assuming a mind behind fluent words and distinguishes chatbot understanding from human understanding, but does not identify expecting them to track one another as an anthropomorphic mistake.
